slides.title: Case Overview: BP vs Buckler (1987)
slides.content:
The 1987 case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler concerned Great House Farm, Llandough — property long occupied by the Williams/Buckler family. The court ruled against the family based on the argument that Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler (referred to as 'Mrs Buckler' in court documents) did not formally reject an offer made by BP Properties Ltd, treating that as tacit acceptance.

However, she had already explicitly rejected prior licence attempts by BP Pension Trust Ltd, a related BP entity. The judge ruled that BP Properties Ltd was a distinct legal entity, making her prior rejection legally irrelevant. Later, in her son's appeal, the court dismissed the appeal, ruling that 'BP companies are all effectively one and the same.'

This contradictory reasoning — treating the companies as separate when it benefited BP, but as the same when it benefited the Bucklers — represents a procedural inconsistency amounting to bias, which may justify reopening under CPR 52.30 and Limitations Act Section 32.

slides.title: Historical Timeline
slides.content: Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, is described in the HER record GGAT02038s as a post-medieval farm, with architectural features and a possible medieval core discussed in the cited source material. The Williams/Buckler family claim occupation from 1667. Other key dates include the 1877 parcel split, 1916 agricultural tenancy, the 1955 possession proceedings concerning Parcel B, the 1974 H. J. Thomas survey, the 1982 land-registration records, the 1986 trial and 1987 appeal in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler, demolition on 6 December 1988, the Strasbourg application registered in December 1988 and declared inadmissible on 14 April 1989, and outline planning permission 89/01396/OUT granted on 13 March 1990. Dates and legal characterisations should be checked against the linked primary records.

slides.title: 1974 Heritage Survey, 1988 Demolition and Strasbourg Evidence
slides.content:
The HER entry GGAT02038s cites R. F. Suggett’s December 1988 note and refers to H. J. Thomas’s 1974 survey of Great House Farm. The reported survey observations concern historic architectural features and a possible medieval core, with access limitations noted. The 1974 survey predates demolition on 6 December 1988; the Suggett note itself postdates the demolition. Heneb reportedly said in October 2026 that the underlying HER source file had been digitised and uploaded to Archwilio. The HER entry’s earlier public citation must be distinguished from access to the underlying source documents.

This raises a specific research question for the family’s European Commission of Human Rights application 14464/88: was the 1974 survey or its findings known to the family and their representatives, and was it included in the submissions? The application was registered in December 1988 and declared inadmissible on 14 April 1989. The surviving evidence identified so far does not establish what the Commission received or that the outcome would have differed.

Historic significance did not automatically confer Grade II listing or prove demolition unlawful. Compare the original 1974 survey, Suggett note and source-file metadata, Cadw’s listing/spot-listing records, surviving family or legal papers, the Commission decision, and planning records. Related records: https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/ghf-e137-1974-h-j-thomas-rcahmw-architectural-survey-and-floor-plan/ ; https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/ghf-e183-heneb-her-source-file-request-and-replies-september-october-2026/ ; https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/ghf-e184-heneb-schedule-of-records-and-16-october-response/ ; https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/ghf-e145-echr-application-14464-88-and-commission-decision-14-april-1989/.

slides.title: Bute Estate Chain of Title
slides.content:
The Bute Estate Records (Series D 219, NLW) show manorial leases from 1552-1829 treating the Bute/Pembroke estate as superior landholder. The 'Llandough manorial leases and agreements' explicitly covers Great House Farm (c. 166 acres). An 1820 memorandum shows Bute taking control of farms including 'Great House Farm alias Cedfin'.

Family testimony states a 1667 acquisition and a later Daniel Thomas/Bute deal in the early 1900s allowing quarrying in exchange for title. The missing deeds referred to in court records — allegedly stolen from Cardiff Library in 1984 — would prove this chain. The 1900s conveyance would shift legal framing from occupation to ownership.
